item.title: Between old walls, new stories grow
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
For centuries, waterways have wound through downtown Suzhou in Jiangsu province, passing traditional houses with black-tiled roofs and whitewashed walls. Visitors flock to the city's celebrated classical gardens, nine of which are on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Yet just minutes from the tourist hotspots, narrow alleys conceal homes whose histories time has gradually blurred. During the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties, Suzhou was a major economic hub. Its historic Gusu district remains home to former residences of officials, scholars and wealthy merchants. But erosion, neglect, termite damage, and successive alterations have taken their toll. Many once-grand mansions were divided among several families, leaving residents with cramped and often uncomfortable living conditions. A major restoration project in Gusu began in 2024 and is now nearing completion. It covers 231 historic buildings, none of which has been formally designated as a protected heritage site at the national, provincial or municipal level. Of these, 189 will remain residential compounds after restoration. The project is supported by the Ministry of Finance, the National Cultural Heritage Administration and the China Foundation for Cultural Heritage Conservation. It received 50 million yuan ($7.5 million) from national welfare and sports lottery proceeds, with local government departments contributing another 350 million yuan. "Through minimal intervention, we hope to ensure the safety of these cultural heritage sites while retaining the everyday bustle of this historic neighborhood," says Xu Yunhe, director of the Cultural Heritage Protection and Management Center of Gusu district. "An ancient city is far more than a vast scenic area for tourists," Xu adds. "What happens today will become history in the future. Heritage protection must also give local residents greater dignity and make their homes more livable." Better places to live Chen Jun, 83, is a retired Peking Opera performer. He moved into an approximately 200-year-old house near Ganjiang East Road after getting married half a century ago. Once owned by the Zhang family, the grand residence is now shared by Chen and several other families. Chen is fortunate that his portion includes a small garden in the backyard. He grows flowers there and sometimes enjoys a leisurely summer afternoon beneath an old tree. Winter in Suzhou, however, is another story. The city's damp, cold weather made poorly sealed windows and a leaking tiled roof a persistent source of discomfort for decades. "My home is not a garden," Chen recalls telling the restoration team. "People enjoy visiting Suzhou's gardens, but they are not designed for modern living. Renovation should serve cultural heritage, but it should also serve the people." Restoration experts considered residents' concerns. The latest work repaired the roof and the garden's pebble-paved ground, while messy electrical wires were neatly routed through dedicated conduits. More importantly, they replaced the original wooden-framed windows with modern alternatives. Xia Jian, a professor of urban planning at Suzhou University of Science and Technology and director of the Suzhou Institute for the Conservation of National Historic Cities, drew up the renovation plan for the compound. He also set aside a room for community activities, giving designers a place to work on site and better understand residents' concerns. Thanks to the residents, the building's main structure has remained relatively intact. "People built up new walls to separate different families," Xia explains. "Indeed, it changed the original layout, but it also reinforced the ancient wooden frames. Residents took care of their homes in their own way. Otherwise, the entire building might have collapsed." More than 20 families still live in the compound, although some have chosen to move out. The vacant rooms are earmarked for conversion into bookstores, guesthouses, exhibition halls, and other cultural facilities. "This will allow the community to develop into a dynamic, mutually supportive environment," Xia says.

item.title: China's foreign trade grows 20% in first 10 months
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
China's foreign trade sustained robust growth in the first 10 months of 2026, with total goods imports and exports rising 20 percent year-on-year to 44.81 trillion yuan ($6.67 trillion), the General Administration of Customs said on Tuesday. Exports increased 17.6 percent to 25.99 trillion yuan, while imports expanded 23.6 percent to 18.82 trillion yuan during the period, data from the administration showed. October marked the sixth consecutive month of double-digit year-on-year growth in both exports and imports, the administration said. The country's goods trade rose 31.2 percent year-on-year to 4.87 trillion yuan last month.

item.title: Xiamen section of Xiamen-Jinmen Bridge joined
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
The Xiamen section of the Xiamen-Jinmen Bridge in Fujian province was joined on Tuesday morning, ahead of a scheduled year-end opening. Builders hoisted the final 3,318-metric-ton steel box girder into place using a 5,500-ton floating crane, before fine-tuning its alignment with synchronized hydraulic jacks. The newly linked span is the final segment of the 14.2-kilometer offshore mainline. Crews are now paving the deck, installing electromechanical components, and working on traffic safety. Totaling 19.6 kilometers, the Xiamen section integrates the offshore bridge, branch links, and onshore tunnels. Its cross-sea main route features a dual eight-lane highway designed for speeds up to 100 km per hour. Once open, the bridge will slash travel time between Xiamen Island and Dadeng Island — home to the new Xiamen Xiang'an International Airport, also set to begin operations by year-end. Designed as a direct cross-Strait transport corridor linking Xiamen and Jinmen, the full bridge project is planned to extend from Xiamen Island via Dadeng Island to Jinmen Island to strengthen cross-Strait connectivity.

item.title: Shanghai's key role highlighted at expo
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
Further facilitating the circulation of key market factors and advancing institutional opening-up is crucial to Shanghai, which has served as the country's major window to the world for years, experts said. They made the comments on Friday, when the Annual Report on the Development of Shanghai Opening-up was released as part of the 9th China International Import Expo, held in the city from Nov 5-10. The city's greater importance attached to the circulation of key market factors can be mirrored by its rising exports of artificial intelligence tokens. Shanghai also accounts for more than half of the country's data broadband exports, according to the report released for the first time this year. Shanghai Mayor Zhu Zhongming said during a city promotion conference on Friday that token exports will be a major development focus in the Lin-gang Special Area over the next few years. These achievements can be largely attributed to Shanghai's multitudinous infrastructure facilities, such as the international data hub in Lin-gang, the international board of the data exchange that includes 30-plus data merchants and nearly 200 data products for trading, as well as the nationally integrated intelligent computing scheduling platform, said the report. To further facilitate the circulation of key factors, Shanghai can explore introducing a "regulatory sandbox" — a setup wherein firms wanting to test new products operate in the market with real consumers — covering data flows and set up comprehensive pilot programs for international data experiments, said Xu Zhanchen, head of the world economy research department at the China Center for International Economic Exchanges. Serving as China's first stop for foreign investment for years, Shanghai has diverted its focus from attracting investment to stabilizing foreign capital throughout their entire life cycle in the city. Against the backdrop of shrinking global capital, intensifying geopolitical competition, and rising domestic and international competition for investment, Shanghai should — for security considerations — optimize the mechanisms for data flows. The city should also comprehensively grant market entry and business operating permits to foreign companies, said Xu, who is also editor-in-chief of the report. Shanghai's continued industrial transformation has bred new demand and opportunities for foreign investors who are interested in the city. The complete industrial system in the Yangtze River Delta region, which Shanghai is a core part of, will further enhance the city's appeal to foreign capital, especially in frontier industries such as electronic information, biomedicine, AI, new energy vehicles, high-end equipment and advanced materials, the report said. "Opening-up must be grounded in industries. The overall efficiency of elevated opening-up should by no means be a matter of self-assertion. It should be measured on a global perspective by including today's global North-South relations, South-South relations, global innovative development progress, global governance reform, and, in particular, the contemporary technology revolution best represented by AI. Shanghai should plan for its next opening-up steps by understanding the whole picture, instead of solely focusing on trade," said Xu. While Shanghai already ranked first among cities worldwide in terms of the flow of goods, it should direct its focus to trade in services such as finance, shipping and professional services, which will help the city have more say in the financial sector, said Zhang Juan, deputy director at the Shanghai Institute of Open Economy.

item.title: Dream weavers' misty mountain retreat
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
In Zhouguan village, Guizhou province, a young man from Beijing chipped away at a block of wood using a technique passed down through generations. Several days later, he had completed an unusual creation: a mask depicting Ganon, the final boss of the video game The Legend of Zelda, in the character's dragon form. For Hu Yongwu, a mask carver in his 50s, showing visitors how to create images of video game characters from wood is nothing new. "I have three more Zelda masks here. Want to take a look?" he said matter-of-factly. An increasing number of young people are making their way to the village in Anshun, known for its wood carving, where they spend carefree days among piles of shavings and the thunk of chisels. One visitor, Shi Jiayi, spent four days at Yalan workshop in the village, becoming so relaxed she got to know the neighborhood cats and dogs. The 25-year-old, from Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, worked in livestream e-commerce before quitting her job and traveling alone to Yunnan and Guizhou provinces. She chose to carve a mythical bird called boqi, which, according to legend, devours nightmares and unpleasant memories. "I don't sleep very well," she said with a laugh, pressing her chisel into the wood. For a fee of around 400 yuan ($60), she spent four days making the mask under the guidance of a master craftsman. First, she carved the bird's basic outline, then worked with her mentor to refine the details. The wood was then heated over a fire to draw out the remaining moisture before the mask was painted. With her brushes, she carefully added emerald and other shades of green to the bird's feathers. Life in the village is a far cry from city life, she said. "The good thing about staying here is that as soon as you open your eyes, you're carving wood," she said. In her livestream sales job, she had to keep up with a relentless work pace and a constant stream of information. During her time in the village, her daily routine was much simpler: pick up a chisel, study the grain of the wood and gradually refine the piece in front of her. Spending long stretches focused on a single object gave her a sense of immersion that she had not experienced in a long time. After finishing her work, she posted a photo on her WeChat Moments feed, accompanied by a single line: "I've raised a mythical beast that eats nightmares."

item.title: Hangzhou across 5,000 years: From ancient Liangzhu to the future
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
More than 5,000 years ago, Liangzhu was home to rice cultivation. Besides vast water management system and intricate jade artifacts, the planned city is a testimony to the existence of Chinese civilization at least 5,000 years ago. Today, experts from around the world gathered in Hangzhou to discuss heritage conservation and facilitate mutual learning among civilizations. Join China Daily's digital employee Yuanxi and cultural heritage vlogger Dong Zhen on a journey from ancient Liangzhu to modern Hangzhou.

item.title: COP31 puts implementation of commitments in focus
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
COP31, the annual United Nations climate summit, opened in Antalya, Turkiye, on Monday, with developing countries calling for faster implementation and fairer distribution of climate finance, while pointing out that climate justice must mean turning global commitments into concrete support for communities facing the worst impacts of a crisis they did little to cause. Officially known as the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the conference will run through Nov 20 and is expected to focus on the implementation of national climate commitments, the delivery of the new climate finance goal agreed at COP29, climate adaptation and resilience, climate mitigation and a just transition. Turkiye is projecting COP31 as an "Implementation COP", with the presidency seeking to move climate diplomacy from declarations and targets toward measurable action on the ground. It has framed its approach around a simple principle: "Commitment is a declaration of intent, but implementation is trust." In his opening address at the conference, COP31 President Murat Kurum outlined Turkiye's vision based on three principles: dialogue, consensus and action. He said that COP31 should connect countries' needs with the capital, technology, knowledge and expertise required to address them. "We want COP31 to deliver on that call as an Implementation COP," Kurum said, emphasizing that the final test of climate decisions would be whether they improve people's daily lives. He also called for narrowing the invisible gaps between countries that can secure finance and those that cannot, and between countries able to withstand climate shocks and those left highly exposed. What makes this year's climate gathering special is that while Turkiye holds the COP31 presidency and is hosting the conference, Australia is co-leading the negotiations as "president of negotiations". COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen used the word "faster" seven times in his opening speech, underscoring his call for the international community to accelerate climate action and finance delivery. "Climate change is here. It is not a forecast. It is not a prediction. It is the lived reality for billions of people," Bowen said. He said that progress had been made since the Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015, but "we must move faster". He added that the conference must speed up the deployment of proven technologies, strengthen resilience and improve access to finance. "The countries that need climate finance the most are getting it the least," Bowen said. "Finance must be disbursed faster. More simply. And more fairly." Faster, fairer delivery UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell described COP31 as part of "a new era of implementation". The task was to build on previous agreements while delivering progress faster, he said. "COPs have traditionally sent signals," Stiell said. "But as well as sending signals, COP31 must supercharge solutions." These include solutions to triple adaptation finance, address the difficulties countries face in accessing committed finance, expand renewable energy and reduce methane emissions. Stronger outcomes from the negotiations would help countries convert targets into real-world results, Stiell said. COP31 is also expected to advance implementation of the COP29 climate finance goal of at least $300 billion a year for developing countries by 2035, while working to scale up finance from all public and private sources toward at least $1.3 trillion annually. For developing countries, however, implementation depends on whether finance reaches communities quickly and on fair terms. Payai Manyok John, director for climate change and the national focal person for UNFCCC at South Sudan's Ministry of Environment and Forestry, said that vulnerable countries needed greater support from developed nations. "We want to make sure that developed countries increase climate finance for the least developed countries, particularly for South Sudan and other highly vulnerable nations," he said. He said South Sudan was developing adaptation and mitigation frameworks focused on smallholder farmers, early-warning systems and nature-based solutions. He emphasized that international decisions must move beyond negotiation rooms. "Whatever negotiation that has come here has to be put into policies and also translated from policies to projects," he said. During a recent news conference, Li Gao, China's vice-minister of ecology and environment and head of the Chinese delegation to COP31, said the conference should address the longstanding problems of insufficient emissions reduction and inadequate financial support from developed countries, while helping developing countries implement their nationally determined contributions. Li also called for progress on a road map for developed countries to meet the $300 billion finance goal by 2035 and to triple adaptation finance. He said COP31 should advance the implementation of a just transition mechanism and help narrow the gap between developed and developing countries. For East Africa, where droughts and floods are already damaging livelihoods, the demand is immediate. Rukiya Khamis, East Africa program manager at 350.org, an international climate organization, said: "Across East Africa people are facing the devastating impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause." She added that COP31 must make climate justice a reality. "That means delivering the finance communities need and making fossil fuel companies pay their fair share, rather than asking ordinary people to foot the bill. "We can't wait until COP32 in Ethiopia to fix what needs fixing now. By the time countries arrive in Addis Ababa next year, we should be negotiating deadlines and binding targets, not vague promises full of 'ifs' and 'maybes'." Xinhua contributed to this story.

item.title: Xi's Vision: Why Shenzhen?
item.description:

Xi's Vision: Why Shenzhen?
By Luo Yueya, Du Wenjuan, Song Wei, Xu Wei, Qin Jize, and Zhang Chunyan | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-11-10 10:58

In December 2012, Xi Jinping chose Shenzhen for his first local inspection tour as China's top leader, reaffirming the country's commitment to reform and opening-up, and calling for bold exploration and innovation. Today, Shenzhen attracts entrepreneurs, engineers and scientists from around the world. Why Shenzhen? China Daily host Dylan Walker visits the city to hear the stories of the people who helped build it, and entrepreneurs from around the world, exploring what continues to drive Shenzhen's remarkable capacity for innovation and growth.

item.title: China's tariff move seen as stability boost
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
China's decision to extend the suspension of additional tariffs on goods from the United States is seen to be conducive to stabilizing bilateral trade ties, improving business confidence and providing greater predictability for companies navigating an uncertain global economic environment, analysts and business executives said. The Customs Tariff Commission of the State Council has announced that China will extend the suspension of an additional 24 percent tariff on US imports for two months, starting on Tuesday afternoon, while maintaining a 10 percent additional tariff. At the same time, the commission said China has noted repeated US statements about plans to replace tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, which were struck down by the US Supreme Court, with tariffs under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974. China will closely monitor subsequent US measures and adjust its tariff countermeasures accordingly, it added. Furthermore, the Ministry of Commerce announced on Monday that China will extend by another two months, starting on Tuesday, the suspension of measures against 11 US entities placed on its unreliable entity list in April 2025. Export restrictions on dual-use items involving 16 other US entities will remain suspended for two more months. Chinese companies seeking to conduct business with the 11 entities can apply for approval, while exporters seeking to supply dual-use items to the 16 entities must obtain licenses from the ministry. Applications meeting regulatory requirements will be approved, said a ministry spokesperson. Fu Suixin, an associate researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of American Studies, said greater tariff and trade policy stability would allow businesses on both sides to make investment and sourcing decisions with more confidence, amid global supply chain adjustments, volatile energy costs and changing trade policies. Zhao Minghao, a professor and deputy director of Fudan University's Center for American Studies in Shanghai, said amid persistent differences over trade and technology, sustained high-level dialogue and effective communication mechanisms could help China and the US manage disputes and maintain more predictable economic ties. Despite persistent trade tensions, China-US trade in goods grew 4.1 percent year-on-year to 3.18 trillion yuan ($476.5 billion) in the first three quarters of 2026, data from the General Administration of Customs showed. Wang Ruibin, chairman of Ningbo Sibranch Microelectronics Technology Co, a semiconductor silicon wafer processor based in Ningbo, Zhejiang province, said the duty adjustments and reciprocal tariff reductions can provide greater pricing certainty for businesses in both China and the US. The company imported nearly 4 million yuan worth of silicon wafers in the first 10 months of 2026, up 30 percent year-on-year, according to Ningbo Customs. "US-made products account for nearly 60 percent of our silicon wafer imports, and our finished products are mainly exported to the US, Vietnam and Malaysia," Wang said. For US companies operating in China, bilateral economic ties extend well beyond tariffs. Speaking at his company's booth at the 9th China International Import Expo, which runs through Tuesday in Shanghai, Jeffery Fay, senior vice-president of global product development and consumer strategy at US audio technology company Harman International, said China remains central to the group's global strategy, serving as both a major consumer market and a hub for technological innovation. With 5,200 employees and four research and development centers in China, Harman benefits from the country's advanced manufacturing capabilities and extensive supply chain network, helping the company expand across the Asia-Pacific region and serve customers worldwide, said Fay, who has been based in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, for three years. Christopher Eck, director of the Indiana Soybean Alliance, said that greater predictability in Chinese purchases is welcomed by US farmers grappling with rising production costs, offering an encouraging sign for bilateral agricultural trade. zhongnan@chinadaily.com.cn
